catalog_quote: Takanan languages have complex and still poorly understood accentual systems. The function of these systems is to delimit the phonological/prosodic word; none of them are lexically/morphologically constrastive. ... In the stress systems that have been studied to some degree (i.e., Ese Ejja, Araona and Tacana), stress falls on one of the first three syllables or morae counting from the left. Which syllable/mora receives stress (1st, 2nd or 3rd) depends on a range of different phonological and morphological factors which differ according to the languages. In Tacana, the basic rule is that, underlyingly, most lexemes are stressed on the 3rd mora (vowel or semi-vowel y [j]) from the left. This pattern is revealed on the surface when the prosodic word contains at least four morae, as in (3). sweep_summary: Both sweep items are one work: Van Wynen & Van Wynen 1962 'Fonemas tacana y modelos de acentuación' (Notas Lingüísticas de Bolivia 6, 32 pp., Spanish translation by Liendo Lazarte; Glottolog 131222 and 688467 duplicate it), the only dedicated Tacana stress analysis and the source Guillaume cites for the catalog rule. No open copy of the full booklet exists: the Rosetta Project extracts on archive. 8-16, 22-23) and the word list (pp. 30-32); section 6 'Modelos de acentuación' is missing; SIL archive 10799 says 'Not Available Online'; Google Books shows only citing works; HathiTrust/WorldCat blocked; Harvard holds a print copy (scan-and-deliver eligible). What was read is consistent with the catalog: the stress pattern is keyed to syllable count with vowel sequences as single syllables, and the three stress-marked forms (eaṣéaṣeni, aṣeáṣetaitia, miméa) fall where Guillaume's 3rd-mora/penult rule predicts; but no rule statement was obtained, so the catalog's deciding source (Guillaume 2023/HAL v2 pp. 8-9, re-read and unchanged; Guillaume 2024 fn. 5 adds [w] as a mora) stands. Acquiring section 6 is high priority because Van Wynen's 'according to the number of syllables' phrasing may show a syllable-counting rather than mora-counting analysis, which bears on the weight-hedged coding. updated in the working files.

new_statements.quote: El modelo de acentuación de acuerdo con el número de las sílabas (ver sección 6) corrobora esta interpretación. [p. 12] ... Cuando las vocales bajas /e/ y /a/ se encuentran en combinación mutua entre morfemas pero intermedio de la palabra, se las interpreta como dos sílabas distintas y el acento puede caer sobre cualquier de las vocales. [eaṣéaṣeni] 'estoy cazando'; [aṣeáṣetaitia] 'he cazado'. [p. 13]
new_statements.translation: The stress pattern according to the number of syllables (see section 6) corroborates this interpretation. ... When the low vowels /e/ and /a/ occur together across a morpheme boundary but inside the word, they are interpreted as two distinct syllables and the accent can fall on either of the vowels: [eaṣéaṣeni] 'I am hunting'; [aṣeáṣetaitia] 'I have hunted'.
new_statements.citation: Van Wynen, Donald & Mabel Garrard de Van Wynen (trad. Manuel Liendo Lazarte). 1962. Fonemas tacana y modelos de acentuación (Notas Lingüísticas de Bolivia 6). Cochabamba: ILV.
new_statements.locator: pp. 12-13, section 2 'Interpretación', subsection 'Combinaciones de vocales' (stress marks verified on the page images)
new_statements.reading: First-hand primary source (SIL fieldwork 1956-61), but not a rule statement: the rule itself sits in the unheld section 6. What is read says stress position is a function of syllable count (with vowel sequences /ia ai ua au ie ei ue eu iu ui/ counted as single syllables), and the stress-marked forms — eaṣéaṣeni and aṣeáṣetaitia stressed on the 3rd vowel from the left, miméa (p. 13) on the penult of a 3-vowel word — all agree with the catalog's Guillaume rule (3rd mora from the left in words of ≥4 morae, penultimate otherwise). The 'según el número de las sílabas' wording leaves open whether Van Wynen's own analysis counted syllables rather than morae, the very point behind the weight-hedged coding.

sources.quote: Primary stress is generally on the penult of words without affixes spoken in isolation. When affixes are added new stress patterns occur. From these patterns Tacana words can be classified into three classes:1. stress on the second syllable2. stress on the third syllable3. mixed. (Key 1968:29)

This pattern is revealed on the surface when the prosodic word contains at least four morae and is illustrated in (6) with different types of monomoraic syllables and in (7) with the bimoraic syllable /ja/. When the prosodic word has fewer than four morae, stress surfaces on the penultimate syllable, as illustrated in (8) (van Wynen & van Wynen 1962; Guillaume fieldnotes 2009-2013).'
